visible.summary:
Spain is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. The 2023 "Trans Law" established legal gender recognition by self-identification and broad anti-discrimination protections, and a parallel penal-code reform made gender identity an explicit hate-crime ground — with real enforcement, including convictions carrying transphobia aggravation. There is no legal restriction on trans people using bathrooms or facilities matching their presentation, and the national tourism industry actively promotes Spain as an LGBTQ destination.

Acceptance is high in cities and tourist regions, though attitudes can be more conservative in some rural areas. Political debate around trans rights is heated, and some regional governments (Madrid, 2023) have rolled back regional protections — signals of a polarised climate rather than changes to a visitor's everyday legal position.

Documented incidents exist: harassment and verbal-abuse prosecutions, a high-profile local-police transphobia case in Benidorm, and gangs targeting queer tourists through dating apps (mainly gay men) in tourist zones — the latter being a general safety caution for app-based meetups anywhere.
visible.tangentialFactors: Dating-app predation gangs in tourist zones (mainly targeting gay men) — a caution for trans visitors using apps.
visible.localsOnly: The 2023 Trans Law's self-identification LGR procedure is resident-facing administrative law.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Petty theft in tourist hotspots, drunken nightlife incidents, and general terrorism guidance affect all travellers. Dating-app meeting risks apply to everyone using them.

sources.claim: Official text of Ley 4/2023 (28 Feb 2023), 'real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantee of LGTBI rights', BOE. Article 43: any person of legal age 16+ may request rectification of the registry gender mention themselves before the Civil Registry - the administrative self-identification route visitors and residents use; law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12-16.

Human Rights Watch (16 Feb 2023): parliament passed the 'Trans Law' - gender recognition now by self-identification through a simple administrative process, ending the prior requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Also expands assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans non-consensual 'normalising' surgeries on intersex children, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and adds anti-discrimination measures in healthcare, employment and housing; recognition possible from age 12 under conditions. Joins Argentina, Ireland, Portugal, Uruguay and peers.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (Jun 2026): disentangles which statute does what - 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Criminal Code; the hate-speech aggravation (Art. 22.4 CP) and Art. 510 CP penalties (1-4 years plus 6-12 month fine) come from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 reformed offences against sexual freedom (Arts. 132, 173, 178-181, 189 bis). Useful for reading actual enforcement: gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence.

Euro Weekly News (9 Jul 2026): practical bathroom-access contrast for travellers - the UK is moving toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the EHRC statutory code (restrictions case-by-case, not a blanket ban), while Spain remains committed to a legal framework centred on gender self-determination. Visitor takeaway: facility access rules differ on either side of the Channel.

Intrepid Travel LGBTQIA+ country guide: rates Spain a safe and welcoming destination for LGBTQIA+ travellers, especially tourist hubs Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting attitudes can be more conservative outside big cities and that same-sex marriage plus protective laws apply. Advises knowing local conditions before going (venues, regional variation).

Turespana (national tourism institute) B2B page: names Spain's 8 flagship LGBTQ+ destinations - Madrid (Chueca), Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, Canary Islands (Maspalomas Pride), Sitges and Torremolinos (La Nogalera) - and the 'Destinations for Diversity' certification for open, safe, welcoming, discrimination-free spaces. Practical destination map for trip planning.

La Razon (Jul 2026): Vigo's Tribunal de Instancia applied the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia for the first time, in a misdemeanour threats case - messages threatening a trans woman sent by WhatsApp; the author was fined EUR 300. First instance-level precedent that gender-identity aggravation is being applied in practice.

Observatorio de delitos de odio (8 Jan 2026, reporting Las Provincias): a juvenile gang in a Valencia park harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison, two minors were separately judged. Documents actual sentence outcomes for gender-identity-motivated violence.

UK Foreign travel advice, Spain (safety and security): official UK government view that Spain is 'a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers' with active communities and social venues, alongside standard crime warnings (counterfeit money treated as a serious offence). Baseline official safety framing for a UK-issued passport holder.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex marriage and full adoption rights since 2005; legal gender change without surgery or sterilisation; LGBTQ military service and MSM blood donation since 2005; Spain recognised as one of the world's most LGBT-friendly countries. Backbone timeline for the record.

BuzzFeed News / Ipsos-style 23-country survey (Dec 2016): Spain ranked most trans-supportive of the 23 - the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, restroom support over 70% (with Argentina and India), and 25% of respondents knew a trans person. Dated public-attitude baseline predating the 2023 law.

visible.summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas.
visible.tangentialFactors: Dating-app robbery schemes (documented as fatal for gay men) are a caution for trans visitors using apps.
visible.localsOnly: The name/gender-marker change procedure and the transphobia criminalisation are resident-facing legal machinery; the world's-highest trans murder toll falls on local trans people, concentrated in poor and marginalised communities.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Brazil's general crime problem (armed robbery, express kidnappings, gang violence) drives all governments to advise a high degree of caution for every traveller.

sources.claim: Overview: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013; legal gender change without surgery allowed since 2018 (STF); age of consent equal; plus federal anti-discrimination framework.

Country overview (updated Mar 2026): constitutional and federal criminal provisions — after the 2019 Supreme Court ruling — prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, yet LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination in practice.
Expat legal guide (updated 5 Apr 2026): same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules — the practical family/entry framework a trans visitor or partner needs.
Investigation (May 2024): 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies victimise LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo; the city prepares for a Pride drawing thousands of tourists.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Death threats assail Brazil's trailblazing trans candidates as they campaign' — nearly 1,000 transgender politicians run in municipal elections across every state amid threats and intimidation, as the number of trans officeholders has tripled since the last cycle.

São Paulo Court of Justice (27th Private Chamber) upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing — the Barra Bonita first instance had ordered R$4,000 compensation.

Analysis (2022): lower courts pushed the Superior Court of Justice (STJ) toward unanimously extending Maria da Penha Law and Feminicide Law remedies to trans women — inclusion of trans people in violence-prevention law.
Official page of the São Paulo Municipal Council's parliamentary inquiry (CPI) on Violence Against Trans and Travesti Persons — final report concluded carrying 189 recommendations.

Canada travel advisory (updated Aug 2026): 'Exercise a high degree of caution' — high crime rates and gang-related urban violence; avoid demonstrations and border drug-trafficking zones. Dated country-wide baseline for visitors.
Tour operator guide: Brazil 'progressive' on LGBTQIA+ rights and generally safe, but flags that practical safety issues can arise for LGBTQIA+ travellers.
Historical essay (Mar 2000): historian James N. Green on early-1900s Rio homosexual subculture — Glória monument site functioning as a meeting venue in the 'tropical Paris' era.

visible.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under its uncodified Sharia legal system, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and the morality police enforce with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned.

Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a Pakistani trans woman died in custody in Riyadh in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. Amnesty International reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the Kingdom — and device inspection at the border is an established risk.

The tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment — a catastrophic formal exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Missile and drone attacks on infrastructure, and the general risk of detention without charge for any visitor, affect all travellers.

sources.claim: LegalClarity (4 Jun 2026): Saudi Arabia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity with no codified penal code — judges apply an uncodified sharia interpretation; penalties range from flogging and lengthy imprisonment to death in the most severe cases; visitor-facing explainer of the laws, how enforcement works and rules for visitors.

Outright International Saudi Arabia overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminal penalties are based on Shari'a; same-sex relations illegal for men and women; no legal gender recognition; LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute Saudi Arabia profile (MENA Trans Archives): deviating from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence; regional legal-research framing of gender-nonconformity provisions and their enforcement.

Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Saudi Arabia' (fetched 2026): same-sex conduct illegal with penalties including capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging and fines; no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no same-sex relationship recognition; law uncodified on a Wahhabist interpretation of sharia (Quran/Sunnah), with enforcement-case and living-conditions sections. Reference overview.

BBC News: 'Meeno' — Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman — died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh; Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack; family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. Directly relevant to how Saudi enforcement treats trans people.

Gulf News (25 Oct 2021): five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media — cross-dressing/gender-nonconformity enforced as a criminal matter.

Amnesty International (29 Jun 2026, updated 17 Jul 2026): documents visitors imprisoned over social media posts — including a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 Aug 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for posts published before he even arrived in the country. Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground.

UK FCDO Saudi Arabia safety advice (current): same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon; couples should avoid public affection; VisitSaudi states all visitors are welcome and privacy will be respected; being transgender is not recognised — trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care.

A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map (2024/25): Saudi Arabia appears among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan; page also profiles safest destinations (Iceland: self-ID, marriage since 2010).

The Guardian (April 2005) by Brian Whitaker: 'Saudis' tough line on gays' - dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and 'behaving like women' at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes plus up to two years' jail, after a closed trial without defence lawyers; HRW's Scott Long: 'Prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct are flagrant human rights violations.'

visible.summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since January 2025 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The absent legal gender marker procedure and the weakly enforced 2015 Gender Equality Act are resident-facing; the Pattaya murder and the hate-crime-law gap concern residents primarily.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Scams, drink-spiking in nightlife, road safety, and petty theft affect all travellers to Thailand.

sources.claim: Thai Government PRD (05/08/2024): the Immigration Bureau launched 'Welcome Pride by Immigration' to mitigate concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports don't match their current appearance or gender — the entry-friction fix a trans visitor most needs to know about before arrival.

Outright International country overview (last updated Mar 12, 2026): Thailand became the first country in Southeast Asia to legalise same-sex marriage — bill passed its final Senate reading June 2024, in effect January 22, 2025, using gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms; its at-a-glance tables also carry the legal-status read.

Bangkok Post 'Pride in Action' forum (Lido Connect, 2025): advocates urge the government to expedite a gender-recognition law following marriage-equality, with public education framed as part of expanding rights protection — legal gender recognition is still pending post-SSM.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Nov 2025): when a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April, the community called it a hate crime but Thai law has no hate-crime designation — bias-motivated violence is handled as ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties or data collection; documents the accountability gap.

Globe (05/05/2025): following the Pattaya killing of a Thai trans woman by 42-year-old Chinese citizen Fu Tongyung after she refused his request for sex, LGBTQ+ groups urgently called for new hate-crime protections — names the perpetrator/victim facts and the resulting legal-protection push.

HRW report 'People Can't Be Fit into Boxes' (Dec 2021): no route for transgender people to obtain legal documentation reflecting their gender identity; even affirmative measures like first-name change leave discretionary power with officials; anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced — the documentation gap a trans visitor may also feel.

NZZ in English (May 2025): the conservative government introduced progressive trans laws including free hormone treatments with little public opposition; trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than typical in the West — explains why social climate outruns the legal framework.

LegalClarity (June 2026): marriage equality since January 2025 and anti-discrimination law since 2015, yet no mechanism to change the sex marker on birth certificate, national ID or passport (title prefixes locked to sex at birth; Name Act 1962 partial workaround) — precise current documentation-status read.

Fulcrum/ISEAS (June 2025): analyses the government's push to position Thailand as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub (Bangkok Pride 4 June backdrop) alongside marriage equality — weighs opportunities and challenges of a state strategy whose motives range from genuine commitment to economic opportunism; relevant to how welcoming institutions are pitched to visitors.

G.A.M. Legal Alliance (Thai firm) analysis of the post-same-sex-marriage landscape: marriage equality closes practical gaps for couples — exclusion from property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims — the concrete before/after of the January 2025 change.

GlobalGayz archive (2007-10): index of Thai LGBT news of the era — the National Human Rights Commission's role, constitutional-charter gay-rights campaigns, Phuket acceptance/rejection accounts, and the 'Please call me Miss' debate on trans legal title — historical baseline showing how long recognition questions have been live.

visible.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.
visible.tangentialFactors: Marriage equality nationwide — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The state-by-state administrative LGR regime and the transfemicide statutes (Mexico City, Nayarit) are resident-facing; the 71-murder toll falls overwhelmingly on local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Cartel violence, kidnapping, and theft drive several governments to advise caution or non-essential travel avoidance for parts of Mexico — a risk independent of any personal characteristic.

sources.claim: HRW dispatch (31 March 2025) "Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges": calls on Mexico’s states to guarantee administrative legal gender recognition — many states now have LGR procedures, but without recognition, document requests expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; implementation gaps persist state to state.

HRW report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024), Tabasco: barriers to legal name/gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, set against murders including a trans woman found in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

The Guardian (18 July 2024): Mexico City’s Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" criminalising transfemicide — a watershed named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

AP (Jan 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings in Mexico spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

IACHR press release (2024): urges federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all LGBTI violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

Agencia Presentes (Jun 2024): 'Violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders increased in the last year' in Mexico — data report on rising attacks against trans people and killings of defenders.

LSE USAPP analysis by Caroline Beer (22 November 2024): Mexico’s progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly — rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the authors explicitly caution their earlier work must not be read as evidence LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture.

Global Affairs Canada travel advice for Mexico: "Exercise a high degree of caution" nationwide due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with regional "avoid non-essential travel" advisories (e.g. Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast); recently updated for Hurricane Polo.

Intrepid Travel LGBTQIA+ Mexico guide: same-sex marriage legalised in 2009 with Mexico City the pioneer and Zona Rosa its gay hub (annual Pride, LGBT-friendly hotels/bars/tours); Cancún is a mainstream hotspot; notes Oaxaca’s indigenous muxé third-gender tradition and advises caution outside tourist hubs.

CNN en Español (19 July 2024): Mexico City’s Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro" law criminalising transfeminicide; Transgender Europe monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023 — second only to Brazil’s 100.

Mail & Guardian (13 January 2007): Coahuila became the third Latin American jurisdiction to approve gay civil unions (20–13 vote) after Mexico City and Buenos Aires, barring adoption and custody for those couples; PRI deputy Julieta Lopez called it "a sensible response" to discrimination, PAN called it an attack on the family.

visible.summary:
Brunei's Sharia Penal Code contains one of the world's most explicit trans-specific criminal provisions: Section 198 creates an offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", and the Bruneian government has confirmed in its official guidance that the code applies to all persons in the country including tourists — travel agents are briefed accordingly. A separate indecency provision criminalises clothing that "tarnishes the image of Islam" with fines and imprisonment, and same-sex intimacy carries a stoning sentence (under a formal moratorium since 2019, with whipping and long prison terms actively available).

Enforcement is quiet rather than predatory — no prosecution of a foreign visitor under these provisions has been documented — but the country is an absolute monarchy with heavy surveillance, censorship, and no LGBT organising of any kind, and LGBT Bruneians have fled abroad. The legal exposure for a discovered trans visitor is categorical: no recognition, no protection, and gender expression itself is a written offence.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex intimacy carries a stoning sentence (moratorium since 2019, whipping and long prison terms available) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No current travel advisory flags general security risks; the hazards here are legal, not criminal.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying document is the text of Brunei's Penal Code (hosted by the Norwegian government), including the Syariah Penal Code provisions.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust briefing (April 2019) analyses Brunei's implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, including death by stoning for anal sex and adultery.

BBC (3 Apr 2019): stage 3 of the Syariah Penal Code took effect — stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, 40 strokes of the cane for lesbian sex; homosexuality was already illegal with up to 10 years. The law mostly applies to Muslims (~two-thirds of the 420,000 population); Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957. Freshness check 2026-09-27: still in force, 2019 moratorium on executions intact.

AP (Apr 2019): 'Brunei death penalty moratorium applied to new Shariah laws' — the sultan says the capital-punishment moratorium covers the new Shariah penal code allowing stoning for gay sex and adultery; under the prior law homosexuality was already punishable by up to 10 years.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (April 2019) covers the fear gripping Brunei's gay community after the Sharia penal code came into force.

TIME (Apr 2019): first-person reporting as the stoning penalties took effect — lesbian sex newly exposes women to 40 lashes; theUN and foreign governments condemned the code; sources describe an economy-pain-fuelled rush of the law through a population of ~450,000 and speak anonymously of a climate of fear, with no assurance of enforcement against foreigners.

UK House of Commons Library debate pack (April 2019) on LGBT rights in Brunei: the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 (in force in stages, final stage 3 April 2019) requires death by stoning for extramarital sex, anal sex and abortion; 40 lashes for lesbian sex; amputation for theft. HRW called it 'barbaric'; the UN High Commissioner urged Brunei to halt it.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying SSRN paper relates to Brunei's Sharia penal code.

HRW '#OUTLAWED' global map: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise gender expression; Brunei is one of at least two (with Oman) whose national laws expressly criminalise 'posing as' or 'imitating' a person of a different sex — the record's trans-specific offence, alongside Malaysia's state-sharia analogue.

US State Dept 2017 report: the Syariah Penal Code bans men dressing as women or women dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse', with no known convictions in 2017; 'liwat' between men carries death by stoning if implemented, and the report records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services. Morality provisions (cross-dressing, alcohol, Ramadan eating, religious propagation) were enforced; sharia implementing regulations were still unissued.
